basis:
WHAT THIS FILE IS. The observed ENVELOPE of every entry the speed gate measures, recorded from six dispatches of one tree on the cell that reads it: ubuntu-latest, image ubuntu24/20260927.320, runner 2.337.0, kernel 6.17.0-1022-azure. Each dispatch ran ROUNDS=2 and the two rounds within a dispatch agreed to about 2%; n records the six dispatch-level observations the min and max below were taken from, so if a future re-measurement has the per-round values split out, n and the envelope are re-derived together rather than widened by hand. No number here is invented, and each traces to a dispatch summarised for this file: the runner figures were reported from dispatches of the tree recorded in measured_commit, and the instrument was chosen by the probe in counter.py, not assumed. measured_at is the WINDOW the six dispatches ran in, not an instant: the field guide's rule is that a magnitude claim names its measurement window, and here the window is knowable, so it is recorded rather than replaced with the moment the document was typed.

WHY AN ENVELOPE AND NOT A SINGLE VALUE. CPU seconds exclude steal, so a co-tenant does not reach them — that is what makes them a valid magnitude where elapsed time is not. They are still hardware-dependent: a faster or narrower core runs the same instructions in fewer CPU seconds, and the ubuntu-latest pool spans instance types. Measured here, one tree over six dispatches spread 58.8% (unit suite: 10.287820 - 16.340854), 61.3% (bench.render: 0.055953 - 0.090278), 83.6% (bench.render-impact: 0.770657 - 1.414891) and 60.1% (bench.render-responsiveness: 0.054544 - 0.087334), and the whole vector moved together — the fastest run was 35-40% below the slowest on every entry at once, which is a property of the machine and not of the code. A single stored value plus a budget wide enough to cover that would need a tolerance above 1.0 on some entries, which is not a loose gate but a gate that cannot fire. So each entry records the range it was actually observed over, the head must clear observed maximum x (1 + tolerance), and the down-only ratchet acts on that recorded maximum: an improvement lowers the ceiling, and a regression has to clear the worst machine actually seen.

WHY THE TOLERANCE IS 0.25 IN BOTH POPULATIONS, AND WHAT THE GATE THEREFORE IS. The recorded maximum already contains the entire observed spread, so the tolerance covers what was NOT observed rather than repeating it. 0.25 is a quarter on top of the worst run observed: it will let an occasional worse-than-anything-seen run through rather than red on a machine the pool surprises us with, and it is far below the ~2x that a genuine step change produces. STATED PLAINLY SO IT IS NOT DISCOVERED LATER: this is a STEP-CHANGE DETECTOR, NOT A REGRESSION DETECTOR. It catches a doubled workload and an accidental quadratic. It will not catch a 20% regression, and the phrase 'load-invariant counter' does not license reading it as a sharp budget. Both populations take the same fraction because their ceilings are both 'the worst machine observed, plus a quarter', and the numbers that differ are in the ceilings, not in the fraction.

WHAT IS NOT HERE. `wall` is empty: no wall observations were supplied with these dispatches, so the gross smoke gate is off rather than armed against a guessed number. When wall figures are collected they go in that map, and the smoke gate starts comparing against them without any other change.

HOW TO RE-DERIVE. Run the job several times on the cell that will read it — at least three, since a two-dispatch envelope is thin — and take each entry's min and max across those dispatches, with n counting them. Re-derive, never carry: an envelope recorded on one machine and applied to another is the mistake this schema exists to make impossible, and it is why the ratchet refuses any raise to a recorded maximum.

PROVENANCE OF measured_commit. d051020 is the REMOTE head the six dispatches resolved against, not a local checkout: the dispatches ran `--ref issue-81-82` against the remote, whose head was d051020 at the time. The local branch was later rewritten in place onto an identical tree by this round's commits, so a future reader diffing SHAs and finding d051020 is not an ancestor of the current head will conclude the file is stale. It is not — the tree it was measured against is the tree this branch still carries, and the commit is recorded because it is the handle the dispatches used, not because it is where the work stopped.

THE SMOKE GATE, AND WHY ITS CEILING IS AN ENVELOPE TOO. `wall` is armed, not empty: an unarmed gate cannot catch a workload that gets slower in wall while CPU holds flat, and that is a real class — blocking on I/O, a network call, a lock wait. The figures are the per-run minima recovered from the six dispatches' gh-wall attributes, which is the same basis as the CPU envelope above.

They spread 52-63% min-to-max (0.056-0.091, 1.011-1.541, 0.055-0.088) — the machine dominates wall and CPU alike on this cell, which is precisely why wall appears here as a gross smoke BOUND and never as a budget. `wall` is an envelope for the same reason `entries` is: with a spread that wide, a single stored figure would be an arbitrary pick among min, median and max, and the wrong pick either trips the gate on noise or leaves it deaf. The gate compares against the recorded maximum, so SMOKE_FACTOR is a multiple of the worst wall actually observed — the right base for a cliff detector — and the report still prints no elapsed time at all.

WHAT IS STILL UNARMED. The unit-suite population's `wall` map is empty: no wall observations were supplied for counter::unit-suite in those dispatches, so the gross smoke bound covers the renderer workloads only. It is empty rather than guessed, and filling it is a line, with no other change and no re-derivation of anything else.
